newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition to carry on despite warning.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition to carry on despite warning.

text.p: Serbian opposition leaders vowed to continue street protests against President Slobodan Milosevic on Monday after authorities issued a warning against further demonstrations.
Milosevic raised the stakes in the confrontation with the opposition when police and city authorities warned they would no longer take a "tolerant" approach to street protests.
Police in the capital Belgrade said recent demonstrations contained "elements of violence and serious violations of the law", the state news agency Tanjug reported.
The police warning coupled with a vitriolic attack broadcast on state television against the opposition signalled that Milosevic's patience was wearing thin after two weeks of protests.
The wave of demonstrations was sparked by the annulment of opposition victories in municipal polls on November 17.
The protests, joined by striking university students, have posed an unprecedented challenge to Milosevic's nine-year rule and damaged his bid to rehabilitate himself with Western powers.
Zoran Djindjic, a leader of the Zajedno (Together) coalition, dismissed the police warning as an attempt to scare people off the streets.
"I see it as a threat directed at the people to stop them from attending the protests in large numbers," Djindjic told Reuters late on Sunday.
"More and more people came to the protests every day and that is a big problem for Milosevic....I think it will have the opposite effect, that even more people will come."
He said Zajedno had no intention of calling off the demonstrations and said strikes in industrial centres may be launched soon.
"We shall bring the political crisis to the boiling point."
Zajedno marches have been mainly peaceful except for a few days in which protesters threw stones at the state television and state newspaper offices, shattering windows.
Opposition stewards managed to put a stop to the stone throwing since Thursday and demonstrators since then have hurled eggs at the two buildings -- symbols of Milosevic's authoritarian rule.
Independent B-92 radio reported on Sunday night that police officers were concerned about the loyalty of some policemen.
The opposition alleges police in Kraljevo, southwest of Belgrade, have pledged not to strike at local residents in any confrontation.
Authorities have sent police to other towns during the demonstrations to avoid any such conflict, local independent media reported.
The speaker of parliament from the ruling socialist party, Dragan Tomic, branded the opposition as "fascist".

Resorting to hardline communist rhetoric, Tomic told state television: "These are not quiet demonstrations as the organisers presented them. These are destructive, massive demonstrations, with all elements of pro-fascist grouping and ideologies."
Tomic compared Zajedno with Adolf Hitler's Nazis.

"Remember when Hitler came to power, remember before he came to power, that is what he did also. Everything is being said in the name of democracy and each time violence is invoked. Belgrade is now being destroyed."
Milosevic's socialists have already cracked down on independent media, jamming radio B-92's signal and journalists at state papers have complained of censorship.
Tens of thousands took to the streets again on Sunday despite bitter cold and sleet.
The Belgrade march was smaller than previous protests due to the weather. Saturday's demonstration in the capital drew some 100,000 people.
Zajedno leaders said they planned to stage a boycott of parliament on Tuesday unless the body annuls the local elections which they accuse the socialists of rigging.
